coherence.reasons: Both lead with the same answer and support it with a consistent chain from market to unit economics to customers to cash to alternative. Y groups its argument into three mutually reinforcing pillars (economics fail, cannot afford to find out, software is the better route), and each slide title carries a quantified claim that rolls up to its pillar. X's five sub-questions also form a sound hierarchy, but a few titles and claims sit awkwardly with their evidence. Slide 12's title says orders 'pay their own way' on a before-site-cost basis while the governing metric is after site costs. Slide 10 claims a loss 'even before the dark store is paid for' but cites the after-site-cost figure. The difference is small.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation (do not launch, scale software, sell store-based fast delivery to grocers, with reopening gates), and both reject the one-store pilot on runway grounds. Y weighs the alternatives more fully. It compares four options plus a second pop-up and a hybrid against five criteria, including downside and reversibility. It stress-tests the recommended software path at 45% and 30% growth and with rising opex, and names a pre-agreed cost action if growth slips. It also flags founder focus as an execution risk. X compares three options against four tests and rests the software path on a single 60% growth case, with the assumption disclosed but not tested. X's gates are sensible, and its point about becoming a rival to grocer customers is well made, though Y makes it too. Y's reopening trigger of 'no extra fee' is somewhat arbitrary given the Zipcart evidence, but this is a minor flaw.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the key calculations correctly: −$6.17 at the median, −$1.76 at the best composite, −$12.57 for the pop-up, a $63 break-even basket at the median, about 15 months CAC payback on plan economics, and −$1.05 with Zipcart's levers. Y adds the grid at best observed density (−$3.44 at the median basket, and a break-even basket of about $50 at best density and best rider productivity), which directly tests the 'density fixes it' claim. Y also states the 41.5% CAGR explicitly and models both readings of the $9.5M budget. X is slightly more cautious on untested claims, for example saying 'nobody owns the Midwest' cannot be tested. Y's '$37M first-year need' and its headline 'cash out in month 15' rest on assumptions it chose (CAC to fill stores, budget on top of software burn), though these are disclosed and the alternative reading is tested. Y's 'more likely a warning than a gap' is a mild overreach. Neither computes that Zipcart's levers at best observed density would turn positive, so both engage with the Zipcart evidence only at the median. On balance Y uses the critical evidence somewhat more completely.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis on the right grounds: the plan needs every driver above the best observed site, the pop-up was below the median on all four, and growth does not equal profit. Y handles the hypothesis more explicitly. It restates the founders' view, sets out five conditions that would have to be true, and gives a verdict on each, granting that the growth claim holds (41.5% CAGR) while showing the rest fail. It directly tests 'we run them better than anyone' against the pop-up, gives fair caveats on the six-week test, and addresses the Zipcart proof point as the founders' own evidence. X does the same work implicitly and also concedes the growth claim and treats Zipcart fairly, but it does not frame the analysis as a test of the founders' claims and leaves the 'run them better' claim less squarely addressed.

overall.reasons: Both documents are strong, numerically sound, and land on the defensible recommendation with measurable reopening gates. Y would serve the board better for four reasons. It tests the founders' case condition by condition. It shows that losses persist even at the best observed density. It handles the budget ambiguity under both readings. And it stress-tests the recommended software path with a clear contingency, so the board sees the risk in the alternative as well as in the launch. X is careful and honest about its limits but leaves the software path on a single growth case and gives a narrower comparison of options.
